subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: Prove that C₀·Cᵣ + C₁·Cᵣ₊₁ + C₂·Cᵣ₊₂ + … + Cₙ₋ᵣ·Cₙ = ²ⁿCₙ₊ᵣ for 0 ≤ r ≤ n. Hence deduce that (i) C₀² + C₁² + C₂² + … + Cₙ² = ²ⁿCₙ and (ii) C₀C₁ + C₁C₂ + C₂C₃ + … + Cₙ₋₁Cₙ = ²ⁿCₙ₊₁.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — the two expansions you multiply, why their product is (1 + x)²ⁿ, which power of x you compare on both sides, and how r = 0 and r = 1 give the two deductions.
insider_note: Write the SAME expansion twice, once in rising and once in falling powers, so the product is (1 + x)²ⁿ. The deductions cost one mark only as substitutions — r = 0 for (i), r = 1 for (ii) — never as fresh proofs.

steps.label: Write the two expansions
steps.margin_note: First two marks. (1 + x)ⁿ in rising powers, and the SAME expansion written as (x + 1)ⁿ in falling powers. Both are the same polynomial; only the order of writing differs.
steps.memory_tip: Write the SAME expansion twice — rising as (1 + x)ⁿ and falling as (x + 1)ⁿ.

recall.must_convey: That (1 + x)ⁿ is written in rising powers of x and (x + 1)ⁿ in falling powers, with the same coefficients C₀ … Cₙ.
accept: write one plus x to the n in rising powers and x plus one to the n in falling powers
the first expansion is C nought plus C one x and so on, the second is C nought x to the n plus C one x to the n minus one and so on
same binomial written two ways, ascending and descending powers
one plus x power n ni rising powers lo, x plus one power n ni falling powers lo rayali
two expansions with the same coefficients but opposite order of powers

steps.why: Multiplying a rising expansion by a falling one is what makes products Cₖ·Cₖ₊ᵣ appear together at a single power of x. That pairing is the whole idea.
common_mistakes: Writing (x + 1)ⁿ with the same rising order as (1 + x)ⁿ, so no useful pairing happens.
Using different letters for the coefficients of the second expansion.

steps.label: Multiply and identify
steps.margin_note: Third and fourth marks. The product is (1 + x)ⁿ(x + 1)ⁿ = (1 + x)²ⁿ — the left side is a big bracket product, the right side a single binomial whose coefficients are ²ⁿCₖ.
steps.memory_tip: The product is (1 + x)ⁿ(x + 1)ⁿ = (1 + x)²ⁿ, whose coefficients are ²ⁿCₖ.

recall.must_convey: That multiplying the two expansions gives (x + 1)ⁿ(1 + x)ⁿ, which is (1 + x)²ⁿ.
accept: multiply the two expansions, the product is one plus x to the two n
x plus one to the n times one plus x to the n is one plus x to the two n
the product of the two brackets equals one plus x to the power two n

left side is the product of the brackets, right side is one plus x to the two n

steps.why: The same product has two forms: a long bracket product whose coefficients are sums of Cₖ·Cⱼ, and a single binomial whose coefficients are known. Comparing them is what proves the identity.
common_mistakes: Writing the product as (1 + x)ⁿ² or (1 + x²)ⁿ.
Trying to expand the bracket product fully instead of picking one power of x.

steps.label: Compare the coefficient of xⁿ⁺ʳ
steps.margin_note: Fifth and sixth marks. On the left, xⁿ⁺ʳ comes from Cₖxⁿ⁻ᵏ (falling) times Cₖ₊ᵣxᵏ⁺ʳ (rising) for k = 0, 1, …, n − r. On the right it is ²ⁿCₙ₊ᵣ.
steps.memory_tip: On the left xⁿ⁺ʳ comes from Cₖxⁿ⁻ᵏ times Cₖ₊ᵣxᵏ⁺ʳ; on the right it is ²ⁿCₙ₊ᵣ.
lines: Right: the coefficient of xⁿ⁺ʳ in (1 + x)²ⁿ

recall.must_convey: That the coefficient of xⁿ⁺ʳ on the left is C₀Cᵣ + C₁Cᵣ₊₁ + … + Cₙ₋ᵣCₙ and on the right is ²ⁿCₙ₊ᵣ, so they are equal.
accept: compare the coefficient of x to the n plus r, on the left it is C nought C r plus C one C r plus one up to C n minus r C n, on the right it is two n C n plus r
pick out x to the n plus r from both sides
the coefficient of x to the n plus r in one plus x to the two n is two n C n plus r

each pair C k times C k plus r gives x to the n plus r

steps.why: Two equal polynomials have equal coefficients for every power. Choosing the power xⁿ⁺ʳ is what makes the lower indices differ by exactly r.
common_mistakes: Comparing xⁿ when the question has a general r.
Writing the right side as ²ⁿCᵣ.

steps.label: Deduce (i) and (ii)
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. r = 0 makes every product a square; r = 1 makes the indices consecutive.
steps.memory_tip: Both deductions are substitutions, not new proofs: r = 0 for (i), r = 1 for (ii).
lines: (i) Put r = 0: C₀² + C₁² + C₂² + … + Cₙ² = ²ⁿCₙ

recall.must_convey: That r = 0 gives the sum of squares equal to ²ⁿCₙ, and r = 1 gives the sum of consecutive products equal to ²ⁿCₙ₊₁.
accept: put r equal to zero to get the sum of squares equals two n C n and r equal to one to get the consecutive products equal two n C n plus one
r zero gives C nought squared plus C one squared and so on equals two n C n

steps.why: The general identity holds for every r from 0 to n, so the two named results are two of its special cases and need no fresh proof.
common_mistakes: Re-proving (i) from scratch instead of substituting r = 0.
Writing (ii) with ²ⁿCₙ on the right.
